caption.p: Full test metrics on MIST PubChem retrieval benchmark

table-wrap-foot.p: The ‘Top k’ columns stand for the retrieval accuracy@k metrics reported in percents (higher is better). ‘Cos. similarity’ shows the cosine similarity (higher is better) between predicted and ground-truth fingerprints (that is, inverted test loss). Methods with the ‘fingerprint’ suffix denote the methods directly predicting molecular fingerprints, whereas ‘contrastive’ means that the training procedure involves batches of PubChem molecules with the same molecular formula and learns to correctly rank candidates via a noise contrastive estimation (NCE) loss function32. We do not experiment with the contrastive extension for our model because it outperforms contrastive methods on top 1 and top 5 metrics without considering additional PubChem molecules. Interestingly, DreaMS underperforms MIST in terms of the cosine similarity despite performing better in retrieval. A similar performance on the same benchmark is observed with SIRIUS, which outperforms MIST in retrieval despite being less accurate in fingerprint prediction32.

caption.title: Benchmarking of MS/MS clustering with LSH and DreaMS embeddings.
caption.p: a, The figure evaluates locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) clustering of MS/MS spectra (n = 94,837 spectra) under varying m/z bin widths and numbers of hyperplanes. As shown, increasing the number of hyperplanes improves LSH clusters in approximating cosine similarity and preserving precursor m/z values, while more spectra remain unclustered. Notably, the m/z bin width has a minor effect on the cluster quality but substantially influences the algorithm’s running time. b, The leftmost column demonstrates the performance of LSH clustering (30 hyperplanes and bin width of 1.0) in grouping spectra from identical compounds. The bars show median values, while error bars represent the corresponding interquartile ranges (n = 94,837 spectra). The remaining bars illustrate the combination of LSH clusters into larger clusters to construct the DreaMS Atlas. The grouping is based on the breadth-first search (BFS) aggregations in the k-NN graph of the DreaMS Atlas under different DreaMS similarity cutoffs. A cutoff of 0.9 enhances the recall of LSH clustering while maintaining a median precision of 1 (second group of bars). Lower cutoffs further increase recall but also introduce more false positives. To ensure that most of the nodes in the DreaMS Atlas represent single molecular structures, we used the 0.9 cutoff for its construction. c, The figure provides an example of a cluster refined using DreaMS k-NN with a 0.9 cutoff, resulting in a precision slightly below 1.0. The cluster contains 30 spectra, of which 28 correspond to the same structure, while two are different but highly similar. Despite the variation, all structures are closely related and exhibit highly similar, potentially indistinguishable, MS/MS spectra. d, The figure generalizes Fig. 3e, quantitatively showcasing the linear organization of self-supervised DreaMS embeddings in the affine PCA subspace with respect to molecular structures, thus demonstrating their robustness to mass spectrometry conditions. In the 1,023-dimensional subspace (embedding dimensionality minus one), the accuracy reaches 0.865 for k = 3 and 0.999 for k = 1, highlighting the linearity of the embedding space in clustering spectra from identical compounds. Additional details can be found in the Online Methods.

caption.title: The pre-trained DreaMS model prioritizes attention to peaks that can be explained by SIRIUS fragmentation trees.
caption.p: The evaluation was conducted as follows: First, we performed a forward pass through the DreaMS model for random MS/MS spectra sampled from the MassSpecGym dataset98 (n = 100,000 spectra). For each spectrum, we extracted attention score matrices across all attention heads and layers, resulting in tensors of shape (num_layers, num_heads, num_peaks, num_peaks). Second, we applied maximum pooling across the number of layers and the number of heads, yielding square matrices of shape (num_peaks, num_peaks), which represent the maximum attention paid to each pair of peaks across the entire transformer model. The green box plots in the figure show the distribution of mean values in these matrices when selecting elements representing the attention scores between peaks with relative intensity not exceeding a certain value (x-axis). The intensity upper bound of 1.1 denotes all peaks, the intensity upper bound of 1.0 denotes all peaks except for the precursor token peak, and so on. Third, we annotated all spectra using SIRIUS fragmentation trees and plotted the attention means when retaining only pairs of peaks that are present in the trees as edges (blue box plots). The figure demonstrates that the attention paid to pairs of peaks, which are explained by fragmentation trees, is significantly higher than the overall attention under different intensity cutoffs (Mann-Whitney U test p-value < 0.05 for each upper bound). In this evaluation, we considered only spectra with more than ten peaks, more than five pairs of peaks after applying the intensity cutoff, and at least 50% of peaks explained by the SIRIUS fragmentation trees. Each box plot displays the median (center line), quartiles (box bounds), whiskers extending to 1.5 times the interquartile range, and outliers beyond.

caption.title: Ablation study of self-supervised pre-training.
caption.p: The evaluated metrics are Pearson correlation coefficients between cosine similarity and Euclidean similarity (the inverse of Euclidean distance) on DreaMS embeddings with Morgan Tanimoto molecular similarity. The bars display maximum values of the metrics achieved through the course of pre-training with each of the model configurations. a, Comparison of different dataset configurations (values in brackets show dataset sizes with ‘k’ standing for thousands and ‘M’ standing for millions). The figure demonstrates that (i) the performance of pre-training consistently increases with the amount of high-quality clustered spectra from GeMS-A10 but (ii) deteriorates when including more loosely clustered spectra (GeMS-A1000 and GeMS-A) or lower-quality spectra (GeMS-B). b–d, Comparison of different DreaMS configurations across three categories: numbers of peaks in each spectrum used for training (b), DreaMS architecture components (c), and modifications of the self-supervision loss function (d). DreaMS represents the final model presented in this work, trained on the GeMS-A10 dataset using the sixty highest peaks, Graphormer-like attention mechanism, Fourier features (5 layers for subsequent feed-forward network), 1024-dimensional embeddings (that is, transformer hidden dimensionality), m/z shift augmentations, masking 30% of m/z values (not masking intensities) sampled proportionally to corresponding intensities, focal loss with gamma equal to 5, retention order prediction, and a 0.05 bin size for m/z labels. Sinusoidal embeddings and tokenized m/z refer to peak representations proposed by Voronov et al.14,25. The underlying dataset comprises pairs of spectra from NIST20 sampled to maximize the entropy of the Tanimoto similarity distribution (n = 5,000 pairs). Data are presented as mean values with error bars representing standard deviations within 1,000 bootstrap samples.

caption.title: Our Murcko histograms splitting of spectral libraries surpasses the structure-disjoint approach.
caption.p: a, Schematic illustration of the Murcko histogram molecular representations. Different molecular structures shown on the right side have identical Murcko histograms shown on the left side. The domain of a Murcko histogram is defined in terms of rings (green structures) of different types based on the number of neighboring rings and linkers (grey structures). The corresponding values are the counts of such ring types. b, Evaluation of data leakage on structure-disjoint and Murcko histogram-disjoint splits of MoNA in terms of the maximum Morgan Tanimoto similarity to each training example computed for each validation example. Structure-disjoint splitting results in many leaking near-duplicate examples present in the validation set (maximum Tanimoto similarity > 0.95) whereas Murcko histograms-based splitting eliminates almost all such examples. The blue pair of structures represents such leaks, and the green pair demonstrates that the high-similarity inter-fold examples resulting from Murcko histogram splitting are rather a result of the imperfectness of Tanimoto similarity than the splitting algorithm. The mean of the Murcko histogram-disjoint similarity distribution is approximately one-half the value of the mean of the structure-disjoint-related distribution, implying that our approach to data splitting is better suited for evaluating model generalization.

caption.title: Extended benchmarking results.
caption.p: a, Cosine similarity in the space of DreaMS embeddings outperforms the supervised method MS2DeepScore and the classic modified cosine and spectral entropy methods, as measured by two metrics: correlation with Morgan Tanimoto similarity and correlation with the maximum common edge subgraph (MCES) distance. b, DreaMS surpasses the other considered methods in an analog search scenario, as measured by the AUROC metric, where positive labels are defined as pairs with MCES distances lower than or equal to a certain threshold. c, Fine-tuned DreaMS demonstrates superior performance compared to other spectral similarity methods in retrieving molecules from spectral libraries, considering a pool of candidates within a 10 ppm mass difference from the query precursor m/z. Importantly, although zero-shot cosine similarity on DreaMS excels in the correlation metrics presented in a, it lacks sensitivity to small structural differences among molecules. This observation motivates us to perform contrastive fine-tuning on challenging examples of molecules with similar masses. d, Left: precursor molecules from the fluorine detection test set shown in Fig. 4j. Right: four most similar training examples to the precursor molecules shown on the left. Details on datasets and metrics are provided in Online Methods.

caption.title: DreaMS embeddings are more robust to the quality of MS/MS spectra than other methods in the context of spectral similarity prediction.
caption.p: Both figures compare the performance of spectral similarity algorithms in terms of pairs where both spectra are either ‘high-quality’ or ‘low-quality’ entries from NIST20. ‘High-quality’ spectra are defined as those satisfying A filtering condition (Fig. 2b; n = 81,699 spectra), while the rest are categorized as ‘low-quality’ (n = 72,861 spectra). Specifically, 98% of low-quality spectra are classified as such because they do not contain at least three peaks with a relative intensity higher than 10%. a, The correlation between spectral similarity scores from different algorithms and the Morgan Tanimoto similarities of the corresponding molecular structures (same evaluation setup as in Fig. 4a). b, Comparison of the algorithms in the analog search scenario (same as in Fig. 4c) showing the AUROC metric for retrieving molecules with MCES distances less than or equal to five. Both evaluations a and b demonstrate that the performance drop on low-quality spectra for DreaMS is substantially smaller than for the other methods. Data are presented as mean values with error bars representing 99% confidence intervals, calculated from 1,000 bootstrap samples.

caption.title: Organization of DreaMS embeddings with respect to various structural properties of molecules.
caption.p: a–f, UMAP projections of DreaMS embeddings for 100,000 spectra from NIST20 visualized as contour plots colored by the number of atoms of different chemical elements. g–k, Identical projections as in a–f, but colored with respect to the topology of molecules. The number of rings and the fraction of atoms with two neighbors characterize the linearity and non-linearity of a molecule. Unlike other depicted properties, the fraction of double bonds is a property depending purely on the connectivity between atoms. Importantly, we show fractions to keep the coloring insensitive to the sizes of molecules, which is typically highly correlated with precursor m/z values of the mass spectra.

caption.title: Additional examples of local neighborhoods in the DreaMS Atlas.
caption.p: a-c, Each graph illustrates a directed four-hop neighborhood of a randomly selected node (pink node outline) in the DreaMS Atlas. Each node corresponds to a DreaMS embedding of an MS/MS spectrum and represents a cluster of spectra obtained using DreaMS and LSH. Node colors represent distinct studies (that is, MassIVE IDs). Edges point to the nearest neighbors and are labeled with DreaMS similarities. The swarm plots on the right display the precursor m/z values for all nodes. a, All spectra originate from the same study characterizing plant tissues but are derived from 34 different plants. They share an identical precursor m/z value up to two decimal places, suggesting that the neighborhood represents a single compound that may be a widely abundant, plant-specific metabolite. b, The spectra display a wide variety of precursor m/z values clustered within a single neighborhood. 98% of the spectra originate from three distinct cancer studies conducted in different laboratories: an early-stage lung cancer lipidomics study (pink), a lipidomic analysis of malignant brain gliomas (yellow), and renal cancer cells study (part of a cluster with 171 spectra). This suggests the presence of a family of lipids that may serve as potential cancer biomarkers. Additionally, four other spectra were identified in studies involving type 2 diabetes, microbial interaction, mice with BAAT gene knockout, and human serum, potentially indicating a broader role for these lipids in processes such as inflammation or immune responses. c, The spectra in the neighborhood primarily originate from diverse human studies, including research on late preterm infants (light orange), human stool (red, light grey), and human body decomposition (pink). Other spectra come from animal-based studies, such as those on pork meat and ApoE knockout mice, or from bile acid extracts (orange, grey). This suggests that this neighborhood represents a primary bile acid prevalent in the human body across different stages of life, as well as in other organisms. The icons were created using BioRender.
